title: Rivers reach the sea
hookLine: the Mundaka ends at the coast: rivers lose their names in the sea, and the knower of Brahman goes home
carry: the knower goes home, like rivers to the sea
last: THE SELF IS SEEN BY A CLEAR MIND.

lines: A RIVER WITH A NAME AND A GODDESS.
cards: The Ganga starts in the Himalayas, under a glacier. For its whole long run it has a name, a goddess, temples on its banks, cities that live by it. People bathe in it, scatter ashes in it, sing to it.
Then it reaches the Bay of Bengal. A few miles out, scoop up a cup of water and try to say which part is the Ganga. You can't.
It hasn't been destroyed. It's arrived. The Prashna used this picture ten days ago, for the sixteen parts.
Today the Mundaka ends with it, and turns it on the one who knows.

teach.h: RIVERS GO HOME INTO THE SEA.
teach.b: Here's Angiras's last picture for Shaunaka. Yatha nadyah syandamanah samudre astam gacchanti nama-rupe vihaya.
As rivers flowing on go home into the sea, leaving name and form behind, so the knower, freed from name and form, goes to the divine person, higher than the high.
Nama-rupa, name and form, is the Upanishads' phrase for everything that makes a thing this and not that: the label and the shape. A river is mostly name and form. Water is water.
What made it the Ganga was the name, and the banks. Astam gacchanti is what the sun does at evening: it goes home, it sets. The rivers don't vanish.
They set into the sea. Then the next verse makes a bold claim. Sa yo ha vai tat paramam brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati.

teach.h: THE KNOWER OF BRAHMAN BECOMES BRAHMAN.
teach.b: Whoever knows that highest Brahman becomes Brahman itself. That person crosses over grief and wrongdoing and, freed from the knots of the heart, becomes immortal. As with the two birds, the schools read it differently.
Advaita teachers take it plainly: the knower is Brahman, and always was; only name and form fell away.
Other Vedanta teachers read becomes Brahman as becoming like Brahman, reaching it, sharing its joy, while the soul stays itself. Both keep the sea.
Many Hindus call this goal moksha, release: in this picture, not being wiped out, but arriving.
Then the Mundaka closes with a bow to its teachers. Namah parama-rishibhyah. Honor to the great seers.

how: The Mundaka closes with 'namah parama-rishibhyah' said twice, so a recitation of the whole text ends by honoring the seers; immersing a loved one's ashes in the Ganga or another river is a common Hindu funeral rite.

o: going home, the way the sun sets
rising, the way the sun climbs at dawn
flowing on, the way a river runs

games.q: rivers and the sea — tap the pairs.
p: they go home, like the setting sun

s: in the verse, the rivers are destroyed by the sea
they go home into it, leaving name and form behind.
the Mundaka says whoever knows Brahman becomes Brahman
brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati, though schools read 'becomes' differently.
the rivers-and-sea image appears only in the Mundaka
the Prashna used it for the sixteen parts (6.5).

games.q: you're a river that has run a long way with a name. you reach the sea. what does the Mundaka say happens?
o: you leave name and form behind and go home into the sea.
you keep your name and flow on top of the sea.
games.why: rivers set into the sea, leaving name and form. so the knower, freed from name and form, reaches the divine person beyond the high.

practice: Say your name to yourself once, then your roles: a child of someone, a friend, a worker, whatever you are to people. Gently set them beside you like shoes left at a door; you'll pick them up again.
For now, rest in what's here without the labels: breathing, aware, simply being, like wide water.

wordCard.voice: Astam, going home, the way the sun sets. The Mundaka's last picture: as rivers set into the sea, the knower, free of name and form, reaches the highest, and becomes Brahman.

orig.note: Sanskrit nāma-rūpa, name and form: what the rivers leave behind in the sea, Mundaka 3.2.8.

carryVoice: Your line: the knower goes home, like rivers to the sea. That's week sixty: fuel in hand, sparks of one fire, om the bow, two birds, truth is the road, a clear mind, and the rivers going home. Day four hundred twenty, done.
